points: HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point, a preventive system that identifies and controls hazards before they can reach the consumer.
A hazard is anything that could contaminate food or harm the consumer.
Biological hazards are micro-organisms, such as food poisoning bacteria and moulds.
Chemical hazards include pesticide residues, cleaning chemicals and metal residues.
Physical hazards are foreign bodies such as glass, metal or bone.
Hazard analysis identifies the hazards at each stage of food processing and assesses how likely and how serious each one is.
A control measure is an action that prevents, removes or reduces a hazard, such as thorough cooking.
A critical control point is a step at which a control measure is essential and can be monitored.

notes.h: The seven principles of HACCP (Higher Level only)
points: Principle 1: carry out a hazard analysis at each stage of the process.
Principle 2: identify the critical control points.
Principle 3: set a critical limit for each critical control point, such as a minimum cooking temperature.
Principle 4: set up monitoring procedures to check each critical control point.
Principle 5: set corrective actions to take when monitoring shows that a critical limit has not been met.
Principle 6: set up verification procedures to confirm that the system is working.
Principle 7: keep records and documentation of the system and its results.

notes.h: Purchase, transport and storage of a hot main course (Higher Level only)
points: Purchase hazards: damaged goods, bacterial or chemical contamination, and pests.
Purchase controls: buy from a reputable shop, and check packaging, use-by dates, temperatures and any signs of pest damage.
Transport hazard: bacteria multiply when food warms up during transport and delays.
Transport control: carry perishable food in cool bags or refrigerated containers, cover it, and minimise the time before it is stored.
Storage hazards: bacterial multiplication and cross-contamination of food.
Storage controls: chill perishable food below 5°C, freeze food at −18°C, and keep raw food separate from cooked food.

notes.h: Preparation and cooking of a hot main course (Higher Level only)
points: Preparation hazards: contamination of food, multiplication of bacteria and cross-contamination.
Preparation controls: wash hands with antibacterial soap before and after handling food, and handle food as little as possible.
Use colour-coded boards and separate utensils for raw and cooked meat, and keep raw meat away from cooked meat and ready-to-eat foods.
Thaw frozen meat or poultry fully, preferably in the fridge on the bottom shelf, before cooking it.
Cooking hazard: bacteria that survive cooking, which can cause food poisoning.
Cooking control: cook thoroughly, turning or stirring the food regularly so that it cooks evenly.
Poultry must reach a core temperature of at least 72°C to destroy bacteria.

notes.h: Serving and reheating a hot main course (Higher Level only)
points: Serving hazards: surviving bacteria multiplying in food that is held too long, and cross-contamination from utensils.
Serving controls: serve cooked food straight after cooking, on a clean plate, with clean utensils.
Hold cooked food above 63°C, and do not hold it for more than about 90 minutes.
Reheating hazard: food that has been cooled and stored can have bacteria that multiply during storage.
Reheating control: reheat food quickly to above 100°C, and reheat it only once.
A marinade used on raw meat must be brought to the boil before it is used as a sauce, otherwise it carries raw-meat bacteria.
HACCP eliminates or reduces hazards, so that food is safer.
It focuses workers on safety at every step of food preparation.
It meets legal requirements and provides written records as evidence of safe practice.
Records help a business plan for future safety, time and cost.
In a catering business, HACCP helps prevent food poisoning outbreaks by controlling hazards from purchase to service.
The system should be reviewed and evaluated regularly.
ISO is the International Organization for Standardization, which publishes internationally agreed standards.
ISO 9000 is a family of standards for quality management systems.
A quality management system uses documented procedures, records and regular internal review to ensure that products meet customer requirements.
Continual improvement of the system is a central principle of ISO 9000.
ISO 9001 is the standard in the family against which organisations are formally certified.
HACCP is a food safety system, whereas ISO 9000 covers quality management in general, and a food business can use both.

keyTerms.definition: A preventive food safety system that identifies hazards in food processing and controls them at critical points.
Anything that could contaminate food or harm the consumer, including micro-organisms, chemicals and foreign bodies.
The identification of hazards at each stage of food processing, and an assessment of how likely and how serious each one is.
An action that prevents, removes or reduces a hazard, such as thorough cooking or chilling.
A step in food processing at which a control measure is essential and can be monitored.
The maximum or minimum value, such as a cooking temperature, that a critical control point must meet to keep food safe.
The action taken when monitoring shows that a critical limit has not been met.
Checks, such as reviews and tests, that confirm a HACCP system is working as planned.
A family of international standards for quality management systems, published by the International Organization for Standardization.
A system of documented procedures, records and reviews used by an organisation to make sure its products meet requirements.

factCards.definition: Biological (bacteria and moulds), chemical (pesticide residues, cleaning chemicals and metal residues) and physical (glass, metal and bone).
Hazard analysis; identifying critical control points; setting critical limits; monitoring; corrective actions; verification; and records and documentation.
It eliminates or reduces hazards and produces safer food; it focuses workers on safety; and it fulfils legal requirements and provides records as evidence.

factCards.term: Five stages of HACCP for a hot main course
factCards.definition: Purchase; transport and storage; preparation; cooking; and serving and reheating.

factCards.term: Minimum core temperature for cooking poultry
factCards.definition: 72°C, held in the centre of the food to destroy bacteria.

questions.prompt: Name the three types of hazard that can contaminate food, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Biological hazard: food poisoning bacteria such as Salmonella, or moulds. Chemical hazard: pesticide residues, cleaning chemicals or metal residues. Physical hazard: foreign bodies such as glass, metal or bone.

questions.prompt: Outline the stages of a HACCP system for making and serving a hot main course, identifying a hazard and a corresponding control measure at each stage.
questions.model: Purchase: hazards are damaged goods, contamination and pests; controls are buying from a reputable shop, checking packaging, dates, temperatures and pest damage. Transport and storage: hazards are bacterial growth and cross-contamination; controls are cool bags, minimal delay, covered food, chilling below 5°C and freezing at −18°C. Preparation: hazards are contamination, bacterial multiplication and cross-contamination; controls are handwashing, colour-coded boards, separate utensils for raw and cooked food, and fully thawing food in the fridge. Cooking: hazard is bacteria surviving cooking; control is thorough cooking with poultry reaching at least 72°C in the centre, turning food regularly. Serving and reheating: hazards are multiplication of surviving bacteria and cross-contamination from utensils; controls are serving on clean plates, holding food above 63°C for no more than about 90 minutes, and reheating quickly to above 100°C only once.
